content: Memory-based self-improving agents—systems that learn from a continuous stream of tasks and enhance their performance over time by maintaining a textual memory bank—have demonstrated significant promise in recent research. However, the reliability of these methods remains underexplored. In this work, we present a comprehensive re-evaluation of two memory-based approaches, expanding the assessment along two key dimensions: (1) conducting multiple runs to quantify performance variance, and (2) randomly shuffling task sequences to evaluate the impact of task order. Our experiments yield two main findings that highlight the fragility of current methods. First, agent evaluation is inherently noisy in complex environments and multi-step tasks, and introducing a self-improving loop can further amplify this noise. Second, the agent’s improvement is highly sensitive to the order in which tasks are presented. Previous studies often rely on default task sequences that create an implicit curriculum, serving as a hidden prerequisite for success. To further investigate this fragility, we manually analyze the agents’ memory and hypothesize that underspecification of tasks and environments contributes to this vulnerability. We test this hypothesis by enriching the memory construction process with more detailed information, such as explicit rubrics and enhanced environment feedback. While this additional information partially mitigates the performance degradation observed in earlier experiments, substantial gaps remain, indicating that other, uncharacterized factors also contribute to the fragility. Moving forward, our work advocates for more rigorous evaluation protocols for self-improving agents, including reporting results across multiple runs and stress-testing under challenging conditions. Additionally, our findings on underspecification highlight the need for systems and interfaces that facilitate effective human oversight, helping to prevent agents from failing in unpredictable ways.
